questions.a: Qoheleth saw that God might give a person wealth and honor so that he lacks nothing that he desires for himself, but then God gives him no ability to enjoy it. Instead, someone else uses his things.

questions.q: If a man’s heart is not satisfied with good and he is not buried with honor, who is better off than he is?
questions.a: If a man’s heart is not satisfied with good and he is not buried with honor, then a baby that is born dead is better off than he is.

questions.q: What does Qoheleth say happens to the stillborn child?
questions.a: Qoheleth says its life is like a mist that fades away, it goes into darkness, and it never receives a name.

questions.q: What does Qoheleth say is true about the stillborn child compared to the unhappy rich man?
questions.a: Qoheleth says the stillborn child never saw the sun or knew anything, but it has more peace than the unhappy rich man.

questions.q: Even if a man should live for two thousand years but does not learn to enjoy good things, what happens to him?
questions.a: Even if a man should live for two thousand years but does not learn to enjoy good things, he ends up dying just like everyone else.

questions.q: Though all a man’s work is to fill his mouth, what happens?
questions.a: Though all a man’s work is to fill his mouth, yet his appetite is not satisfied.

questions.q: According to Qoheleth, what advantage does a wise person have over a fool?
questions.a: Qoheleth says a wise person has no more advantage than a fool, and a poor person who knows how to live well has no great advantage either.

questions.q: What does Qoheleth say is better than always wanting more?
questions.a: Qoheleth says it is better to enjoy what a person already has than to always want more, though even this is temporary and insubstantial.

questions.q: What does Qoheleth say about arguing with someone more powerful?
questions.a: Qoheleth says no one can argue with God, who is more powerful than any person.

questions.q: What happens when many words are spoken?
questions.a: When many words are spoken, they become more meaningless and do not benefit anyone.

questions.q: Who knows what is good for a person during their short life, according to Qoheleth?
questions.a: No one knows what is good for a person during their brief life, or what will happen after them.

commentary.text: The vanity of riches. Also of long life and flourishing families. (Eccl. 6:1-6) The little advantage any one has in outward things. (Eccl. 6:7-12)

Eccl. 6:1-6 A man often has all he needs for outward enjoyment; yet the Lord leaves him so to covetousness or evil dispositions, that he makes no good or comfortable use of what he has. By one means or other his possessions come to strangers; this is vanity, and an evil disease. A numerous family was a matter of fond desire and of high honour among the Hebrews; and long life is the desire of mankind in general. Even with these additions a man may not be able to enjoy his riches, family, and life. Such a man, in his passage through life, seems to have been born for no end or use. And he who has entered on life only for one moment, to quit it the next, has a preferable lot to him who has lived long, but only to suffer.

Eccl. 6:7-12 A little will serve to sustain us comfortably, and a great deal can do no more. The desires of the soul find nothing in the wealth of the world to give satisfaction. The poor man has comfort as well as the richest, and is under no real disadvantage. We cannot say, Better is the sight of the eyes than the resting of the soul in God; for it is better to live by faith in things to come, than to live by sense, which dwells only upon present things. Our lot is appointed. We have what pleases God, and let that please us. The greatest possessions and honours cannot set us above the common events of human life. Seeing that the things men pursue on earth increase vanities, what is man the better for his worldly devices? Our life upon earth is to be reckoned by days. It is fleeting and uncertain, and with little in it to be fond of, or to be depended on. Let us return to God, trust in his mercy through Jesus Christ, and submit to his will. Then soon shall we glide through this vexatious world, and find ourselves in that happy place, where there is fulness of joy and pleasures for evermore.
